prompt: The website commits an `UPDATE` to `stock` and then crashes before sending the event to Kafka. What state is the system left in?

choices.text: The table and the topic disagree, and nothing will repair it
choices.why: Right. Nothing remembers that a send was owed, so nothing retries.

choices.text: PostgreSQL rolls the update back because Kafka never confirmed
choices.why: Kafka is not part of PostgreSQL's transaction; the commit stands.

choices.text: The producer sends the event when the program restarts
choices.why: The event was never handed to the client, so there is nothing to resend.

choices.text: Kafka holds the event in a pending state until the database confirms
choices.why: The event never reached Kafka at all.

prompt: A colleague moves the `produce` call inside the database transaction, just before `COMMIT`. Why does the dual write still fail?

choices.text: Kafka refuses messages sent from inside a transaction
choices.why: Kafka has no idea a database transaction is open.

choices.text: The send succeeds, and then the commit fails
choices.why: Right. Kafka is not part of PostgreSQL's transaction, so that is the Kafka-first failure again.

choices.text: Holding a transaction open while sending makes the event arrive out of order with other events of the same row
choices.why: Order is not the problem the section names; the problem is two writes with no shared transaction.

choices.text: A Kafka transaction around the send would fix it
choices.why: Kafka transactions cover topics, and a database is not a topic.

prompt: Match each approach to what makes the second write.

pairs.right: a relay that reads an events table written in the same transaction
a reader of the database's write-ahead log
the same program, straight after the database write

right_distractors: the broker, from a transaction it shares with PostgreSQL

prompt: Ponto Final's finance team wants each stock change to say which customer reserved the book. Why might CDC on `stock` alone not give them that?

choices.text: Debezium removes personal data from every event before writing it
choices.why: Debezium copies the row as it is; it does not filter columns by itself.

choices.text: Change events only carry the primary key of the row, never its other columns
choices.why: `after` carries the whole new row.

choices.text: The table never held the customer, so its row changes cannot carry it
choices.why: Right. CDC events are row changes, not business facts; an outbox row can carry the fact.

choices.text: Updates are not captured, only inserts
choices.why: Updates are captured, with `op` `u`.

prompt: What is a replication slot?

choices.text: A copy of the database kept on a second server
choices.why: That is a replica; the slot is only a position.

choices.text: A named WAL position kept for one reader
choices.why: Right. It is the database's version of a committed offset.

choices.text: The list of tables whose changes are sent
choices.why: That is the publication.

choices.text: The plugin that turns WAL records into rows
choices.why: That is the output plugin, `pgoutput` here.

prompt: Match each piece of logical decoding to its name in this lesson.
Kafka and PostgreSQL both keep a reader's position. Where do they behave in opposite ways?

choices.text: Kafka deletes old data by retention whether or not it was read; PostgreSQL keeps WAL until the slot confirms it
choices.why: Right. That is why a stopped slot can fill the database's disk.

choices.text: Kafka keeps positions in memory, PostgreSQL on disk
choices.why: Committed offsets are stored durably, in `__consumer_offsets`.

choices.text: PostgreSQL lets several readers share one slot
choices.why: A slot serves one reader; that is what `active` tells you.

choices.text: Kafka positions are bytes, PostgreSQL's are message numbers
choices.why: The reverse: an offset counts messages, an LSN is a byte position.

prompt: A position in PostgreSQL's WAL, written like `0/1A2B3C8`, is called an ___.
Why does the lesson create the publication by hand instead of letting Debezium create one for every table?

choices.text: Debezium cannot create publications when the plugin is pgoutput rather than test_decoding
choices.why: It can; `publication.autocreate.mode` controls it.

choices.text: A publication for every table would slow down every write the database makes
choices.why: The argument in the section is about what leaves the database, not speed.

choices.text: So the CDC user reads only the two tables that leave
choices.why: Right. Naming the tables decides what goes to the broker.

choices.text: Kafka Connect refuses to start without a publication
choices.why: Debezium would create one; the choice is about privilege.

prompt: Why does the lesson restart PostgreSQL after writing `wal_level = logical`?

choices.text: It is only read at start-up
choices.why: Right. Unlike many settings, it cannot be reloaded.

choices.text: Installing Debezium needs PostgreSQL down
choices.why: Debezium is a Connect plugin; installing it touches only files.

choices.text: To clear the WAL the server wrote before
choices.why: A restart does not discard WAL.

choices.text: The `conf.d` directory is read once a day
choices.why: It is read at start-up and on reload, like the main file.

prompt: What is `plugin.path` in Connect's configuration for?

choices.text: It is where Connect writes the offsets of each connector
choices.why: That is `offset.storage.file.filename`.

choices.text: It tells PostgreSQL which output plugin to load
choices.why: That is the connector's `plugin.name`, and PostgreSQL ships pgoutput itself.

choices.text: It lists the topics the connector may write to
choices.why: Topic names come from `topic.prefix` and the tables.

choices.text: The directories Connect loads plugins from
choices.why: Right. Each plugin gets its own class loader.

prompt: Debezium names the topic for the `stock` table `pf.public.stock`. Where does each part come from?

choices.text: Publication, database, table
choices.why: The publication is `ponto_final`; it does not appear in the name.

choices.text: Slot, schema, table
choices.why: The slot is `debezium_stock`; it does not appear in the name.

choices.text: Prefix, schema, table
choices.why: Right: `topic.prefix`, then the schema, then the table.

choices.text: Connector name, schema, table
choices.why: The connector is called `stock`, not `pf`.

prompt: A table with no primary key is added to the publication. What does Debezium lose for it, per the section?

choices.text: The snapshot, which needs a primary key to read the rows of a table one by one, in order
choices.why: A snapshot reads rows with a plain SELECT.

choices.text: A message key that keeps all changes to one row in one partition, in order
choices.why: Right. The primary key becomes the Kafka key.

choices.text: The ability to write JSON
choices.why: The converter does not depend on the key.

choices.text: Its topic, which is never created
choices.why: The topic name comes from the table, key or not.

prompt: `stock.sql` puts every book in every shop. How many rows does `stock` hold before any change?
`curl localhost:8083/connectors/stock/status` shows `FAILED`. Where does the section tell you to look first?

choices.text: In `pg_replication_slots`
choices.why: A failed connector may never have created its slot.

choices.text: In its `trace` field
choices.why: Right. It holds the Java exception.

choices.text: In the `connect.offsets` file
choices.why: That only holds positions.

choices.text: In `kafka-topics.sh --list`
choices.why: Missing topics are a symptom, not the reason.

prompt: The first messages in `pf.public.stock` have `op` set to `r`. What are they?

choices.text: Rows that a transaction rolled back before it committed
choices.why: A rolled-back change never reaches the topic.

choices.text: Replays of messages the connector had already sent once
choices.why: Nothing had been sent before the snapshot.

choices.text: Snapshot reads of existing rows
choices.why: Right. `r` is a snapshot read.

choices.text: Reads made by a consumer
choices.why: Consumers do not write to the topic.

prompt: Match each value of `op` to what happened.

pairs.right: a row read by the snapshot

prompt: An event's `source.ts_ms` and its top-level `ts_ms` are three minutes apart. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The database's clock is three minutes wrong
choices.why: Possible in theory, but the two fields measure two different moments.

choices.text: Debezium processed the change three minutes after the database made it
choices.why: Right. Event time against processing time: the connector is running behind.

choices.text: The message took three minutes to travel from the broker to the consumer that read it
choices.why: Neither field is written by the consumer.

choices.text: The transaction stayed open for three minutes
choices.why: Neither field records when the transaction began.

prompt: A `numeric` price column arrives on the topic as a short string of odd letters. What is the likely cause?

choices.text: The JSON converter has `schemas.enable=false` set on the worker
choices.why: That removes the schema, not the encoding of decimals.

choices.text: The column is corrupt in PostgreSQL
choices.why: `psql` would show the price normally.

choices.text: Debezium's exact decimal encoding, as bytes
choices.why: Right. `decimal.handling.mode` changes it; integer cents avoid it.

choices.text: The publication excludes the price column from the event
choices.why: An excluded column would be missing, not garbled.

prompt: With the default replica identity, the update event for Recife's `bk-02` had `before: null`. Why?

choices.text: The WAL kept only the new row
choices.why: Right. DEFAULT logs the key only when it changes, or on a delete.

choices.text: Debezium drops `before` to save space in Kafka
choices.why: With FULL, the same connector fills `before` in.

choices.text: The JSON converter cannot write two copies of a row
choices.why: The delete event's `before` shows it can.

choices.text: `before` is only filled in on inserts
choices.why: An insert has no before at all.

prompt: A consumer sums `before.qty` over delete events to count copies taken out of the shops. With `REPLICA IDENTITY DEFAULT`, what does it get?

choices.text: The right total, because a delete always writes the whole old row into the WAL first
choices.why: Only the key is logged; `qty` is a placeholder.

choices.text: An error, because `before` is `null` on deletes
choices.why: `before` is there on a delete, with the key.

choices.text: Zero, silently: the WAL kept only the key and `qty` is a placeholder
choices.why: Right. The Natal delete showed `qty` 0 for a row that held 3.

choices.text: Twice the right total, because of the tombstone
choices.why: The tombstone's value is `null`; it has no `before`.

prompt: A message with a key and a `null` value, which tells compaction to drop that key, is called a ___.
Connect is stopped and the database keeps working. What happens to the WAL from the slot's position onwards?

choices.text: PostgreSQL keeps all of it until the slot confirms
choices.why: Right. That is the slot's promise, and its danger.

choices.text: It is deleted after a checkpoint, as usual
choices.why: A slot stops exactly that removal.

choices.text: Only the WAL of `books` and `stock` is kept, and the rest is recycled
choices.why: The WAL is one stream for the whole server; the notes table's bytes were kept too.

choices.text: It is sent straight to Kafka by PostgreSQL, without Debezium in between
choices.why: Nothing reads the slot while Connect is down.

prompt: You set `max_slot_wal_keep_size` to 50GB and the connector is down for a week. What is the trade you made?

choices.text: None: the connector catches up later from the copy of the changes that Kafka keeps
choices.why: The changes it missed were never in Kafka.

choices.text: The database's disk is protected, and the connector must take a new snapshot
choices.why: Right. The slot is marked lost past the limit.

choices.text: The database stops accepting writes as soon as the WAL reaches 50GB on disk
choices.why: It stops keeping WAL for the slot, not taking writes.

choices.text: Kafka's retention is lowered to match
choices.why: The setting is PostgreSQL's alone.

prompt: The published tables change once a day, other tables write all night, and Connect is running. Why can retained WAL still grow?

choices.text: Connect only reads the slot once a day, when the published tables change
choices.why: It reads continuously; there is just nothing for it to confirm.

choices.text: The other tables are captured too
choices.why: They are not in the publication.

choices.text: The slot only moves when a change to its tables is confirmed
choices.why: Right. `heartbeat.interval.ms` makes Debezium confirm on a timer.

choices.text: pgoutput keeps a copy of every table
choices.why: pgoutput decodes; it keeps nothing.

prompt: Put the steps of this lesson's CDC setup in order.
items: Create the roles, the database and the tables
Create the publication for books and stock
Start connect-standalone.sh with both property files
Read the snapshot events from the topic

prompt: A connector was retired last month and its slot was left behind. The database's disk alert fires. What is the right fix?

choices.text: Restart PostgreSQL so it forgets the slot
choices.why: A slot survives a restart; that is its point.

choices.text: Lower Kafka's retention on the CDC topics
choices.why: The WAL is on the database's disk, not the broker's.

choices.text: Drop the slot with `pg_drop_replication_slot`
choices.why: Right. A slot nobody will read again is a leftover.

choices.text: Set REPLICA IDENTITY FULL on every table
choices.why: That makes more WAL, not less.
